content: Traumatic wounds, which result from injuries, can vary significantly in severity. They may range from minor abrasions and small skin tears to more severe injuries involving extensive tissue damage, bone fractures, or even damage to internal organs. This review focuses on two main types of traumatic wounds: those that involve only soft tissue damage and those associated with open fractures, where the bone is exposed due to the injury. In some cases, these wounds are left open and treated with negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT). NPWT is a medical intervention that involves applying a specialized wound dressing connected to a device that generates negative pressure. This negative pressure helps to remove tissue fluid from the wound area. The primary goals of NPWT are to manage the wound, prepare it for further surgical procedures, reduce the risk of infection, and potentially accelerate the healing process, whether or not additional surgical intervention is required. However, there are no systematic reviews that have comprehensively evaluated the effectiveness of NPWT for traumatic wounds. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of NPWT in treating open traumatic wounds in patients across various healthcare settings. To achieve this, a thorough search was conducted in June 2018 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, and EBSCO CINAHL Plus. Clinical trial registries were also searched for ongoing and unpublished studies, and reference lists of relevant studies, reviews, meta-analyses, and health technology reports were examined. No restrictions were applied regarding language, publication date, or study setting. The review included both published and unpublished randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of NPWT for open traumatic wounds, specifically those involving open fractures or soft tissue injuries. The primary outcomes assessed were wound healing, wound infection, and adverse events. Data collection and analysis were conducted independently by two reviewers, who also assessed the risk of bias and rated the certainty of the evidence. The data were analyzed separately for open fracture wounds and other open traumatic wounds that did not involve broken bones. Seven RCTs, involving a total of 1,377 participants, met the inclusion criteria for this review. The sample sizes of the studies ranged from 40 to 586 participants. One study included three treatment arms, all of which were analyzed. Six studies compared NPWT at a pressure of 125 mmHg with standard care, although one of these studies did not report any relevant outcome data. Another study compared NPWT at 75 mmHg with standard care and also compared NPWT at 125 mmHg with NPWT at 75 mmHg. For open fracture wounds, four studies compared NPWT at 125 mmHg with standard care. One study, involving 460 participants, reported the proportion of wounds that had healed in each treatment group at six weeks. The results showed no clear difference between the groups in terms of wound healing (risk ratio [RR] 1.01, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.81 to 1.27). The evidence was of moderate certainty, downgraded due to imprecision. Data on wound infections were pooled from four studies involving 596 participants, with follow-up periods of approximately 30 days. The results were inconclusive, and it remains uncertain whether NPWT at 125 mmHg reduces the risk of wound infection compared to standard care (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.13; I² = 56%). The certainty of this evidence was very low, downgraded due to risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. One study provided data on health-related quality of life, comparing NPWT at 125 mmHg with standard care. The results suggested no clear difference between the two groups in terms of quality of life, as measured by EQ-5D utility scores (mean difference [MD] -0.01, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.06; 364 participants). Similarly, the physical component summary score of the Short Form-12 instrument showed no significant difference (MD -0.50, 95% CI -4.08 to 3.08; 329 participants). The evidence for these outcomes was of moderate to low certainty, downgraded due to imprecision. Moderate-certainty evidence from one trial involving 460 participants indicated that NPWT is unlikely to be a cost-effective treatment for open fractures in the UK. On average, NPWT was more expensive and provided minimal additional quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) compared to standard care. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was estimated at GBP 267,910, and NPWT was deemed unlikely to be cost-effective across a range of cost-per-QALY thresholds. The certainty of this evidence was downgraded due to imprecision. For other open traumatic wounds, two studies were included. One study compared NPWT at 125 mmHg with standard care, while the other was a three-arm study comparing NPWT at 125 mmHg, NPWT at 75 mmHg, and standard care. Pooled data from these two studies, involving 509 participants, suggested no clear difference in the risk of wound infection between NPWT at 125 mmHg and standard care (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.18). The certainty of this evidence was low, downgraded due to risk of bias and imprecision. In the three-arm study, which included 463 participants, data on wound infection were reported for each comparison. It remains uncertain whether there is a difference in the risk of wound infection between NPWT at 75 mmHg and standard care (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.17 to 1.10) or between NPWT at 75 mmHg and 125 mmHg (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.31 to 3.51). The certainty of this evidence was downgraded due to risk of bias and imprecision. In conclusion, moderate-certainty evidence suggests that there is no clear difference between NPWT and standard care in the proportion of open fracture wounds healed at six weeks. Additionally, NPWT is unlikely to be a cost-effective treatment for open fracture wounds. Moderate-certainty evidence indicates that the true effect is likely to be close to the estimated effect, but there is a possibility that it may differ substantially. For other outcomes, such as the risk of wound infection, adverse events, time to closure or coverage surgery, pain, or health-related quality of life, the evidence remains uncertain for both open fracture wounds and other open traumatic wounds.
